title: Over a perfect field, da = 0 in the Kähler differentials exactly for p-th powers a
statement: Let $p$ be a prime number and $k$ a perfect field of characteristic $p$, i.e. a field with $p\cdot1=0$ in which every element is a $p$th power. Let $K/k$ be a field extension [def-pc-field-extension] and $\mathrm d:K\to\Omega_{K/k}$ the module of Kähler differentials of $K$ over $k$ [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials]. Then for $a\in K$ we have $\mathrm da=0$ in $\Omega_{K/k}$ if and only if $a=b^p$ for some $b\in K$. (For example $k=\mathbf F_p$, which is perfect since $c^p=c$ for all $c\in\mathbf F_p$.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031W (lemma-derivative-zero-pth-power) and its proof; tag verified in stacks-project/tags/tags

proof.text: (If.) Let $b\in K$. By the Leibniz rule of the $k$-derivation $\mathrm d$ [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] and induction on $r\ge1$, $\mathrm d(b^r)=rb^{r-1}\mathrm db$ (for $r=1$ trivially; $\mathrm d(b^{r+1})=b\,\mathrm d(b^r)+b^r\mathrm db=(r+1)b^r\mathrm db$). For $r=p$ this gives $\mathrm d(b^p)=p\,b^{p-1}\mathrm db=0$, since $p\cdot1=0$ in $k\subseteq K$. Hence if $a=b^p$ then $\mathrm da=0$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031W (lemma-derivative-zero-pth-power, line 44174); the source proves only the other implication, this one is the computation d(b^p) = p b^{p-1} db

proof.text: ($K^p$ is a subfield containing $k$.) $K$ has characteristic $p$ since $p\cdot1=0$ in $k\subseteq K$. The map $F:K\to K$, $b\mapsto b^p$, is a ring homomorphism: it is multiplicative, and $(b+c)^p=b^p+c^p$ because the binomial coefficients $\binom pj$, $0<j<p$, are divisible by the prime $p$. So $K^p=F(K)$ is a subring of $K$, and a subfield since $(b^p)^{-1}=(b^{-1})^p$ for $b\ne0$. Every $c\in k$ is $c=e^p$ for some $e\in k\subseteq K$ because $k$ is perfect, so $k\subseteq K^p$, and the subfield $kK^p$ of $K$ generated by $k$ and $K^p$ equals $K^p$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Definition Tag 07P1 (definition-p-basis): the compositum kK^p, here equal to K^p as k is perfect

proof.text: (A $p$-basis and the basis of $\Omega_{K/k}$.) $K$ is a field of characteristic $p$ (Step 2), so by [lem-weil-pbc-p-basis-exists] applied to $K$ there is a family $(t_i)_{i\in I}$ of elements of $K$ such that the monomials $t^E=\prod_it_i^{e_i}$, $E=(e_i)_{i\in I}$ with $0\le e_i<p$ and $e_i=0$ for almost all $i$, form a basis of $K$ over $K^p$. Since $K^p=kK^p$ (Step 2), they form a basis of $K$ over $kK^p$, so by [lem-weil-pbc-p-basis-differentials-basis] applied to the extension $K/k$ the family $(\mathrm dt_i)_{i\in I}$ is a basis of the $K$-vector space $\Omega_{K/k}$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 07P2 (lemma-p-basis, line 11363): existence of a p-basis and the implication (a) implies (b)

proof.text:
(Only if.) Suppose $\mathrm da=0$. By Step 3 write $a=\sum_Ec_Et^E$ with $c_E\in K^p$, only finitely many nonzero. Each $c_E$ is a $p$th power, so $\mathrm dc_E=0$ by Step 1, and the Leibniz rule gives $\mathrm d(c_Et^E)=c_E\,\mathrm d(t^E)+t^E\mathrm dc_E=c_E\,\mathrm d(t^E)$. Write $\varepsilon_i$ for the family with $1$ at $i$ and $0$ elsewhere. By the Leibniz rule and Step 1, $\mathrm d(t^E)=\sum_{i:\,e_i\ge1}e_i\,t^{E-\varepsilon_i}\mathrm dt_i$ (a finite sum over the $i$ with $e_i
e0$). Hence $$0=\mathrm da=\sum_{i\in I}\Big(\sum_{E:\,e_i\ge1}e_i\,c_E\,t^{E-\varepsilon_i}\Big)\mathrm dt_i,$$ and since $(\mathrm dt_i)$ is a basis of $\Omega_{K/k}$ (Step 3), $\sum_{E:\,e_i\ge1}e_ic_E\,t^{E-\varepsilon_i}=0$ in $K$ for every $i$. Fix $i$. The map $E\mapsto E-\varepsilon_i$ is injective on the families $E$ with $e_i\ge1$ and takes values in families with entries in $[0,p)$, so the $t^{E-\varepsilon_i}$ occurring are distinct members of the basis $(t^{E'})$ of $K$ over $K^p$; their coefficients $e_ic_E$ lie in $K^p$ (the integer $e_i$ is in the prime field $\mathbf F_p=\mathbf F_p^p\subseteq K^p$), hence $e_ic_E=0$. As $1\le e_i\le p-1$ is not divisible by $p$, $e_i$ is invertible in $K$, so $c_E=0$ for every $E$ with $e_i\ge1$. Every $E
e0$ has some $e_i\ge1$, so $c_E=0$ for all $E
e0$ and $a=c_0\,t^0=c_0\in K^p$, i.e. $a=b^p$ for some $b\in K$. With Step 1 this proves the lemma.

split_report.summary: Statement checked against Algebra 031W (algebra.tex line 44174) and kept. Proof in 4 steps by p-bases (route of the lead's brief, written by an agent; 031W's own proof goes through a separating transcendence basis, colimits of differentials 031G, a finite separable extension with 'computation omitted' and Fields 031V, which would need about five new nodes): (1) d(b^p) = p b^{p-1} db = 0; (2) K^p is a subfield and kK^p = K^p since k is perfect; (3) a p-basis (t_i) of K over K^p by lem-weil-pbc-p-basis-exists, and (dt_i) a basis of Omega_{K/k} by the new node lem-weil-pbc-p-basis-differentials-basis (07P2 (a) implies (b)); (4) expanding a = sum c_E t^E with c_E in K^p, da = sum_i (sum_E e_i c_E t^{E-eps_i}) dt_i, and linear independence of the monomials over K^p forces c_E = 0 for E != 0. One new unsplit node; Mathlib has no p-basis and no characteristic-p statement on Kaehler differentials (searches recorded).
